extracted.intended_audience: authors, translators, and editors of scientific articles to be published in English
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for preparing, translating, and editing scientific manuscripts in English for journal submission, covering structure, language, ethics, and presentation to maximize clarity, completeness, and concision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall principle: Complete, Concise, Clear
rubrics_metrics.description: To make international scientific communication more efficient, research articles and other scientific publications should be COMPLETE, CONCISE, and CLEAR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General aim for all aspects of the manuscript: include all necessary information (complete), eliminate irrelevant/redundant text (concise), and present material so readers can understand (clear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wait until findings are firm
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not begin drafting the whole paper until you are sure that your findings are reasonably firm and complete, allowing you to draw sensible and reliable conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid writing a full manuscript based on preliminary or incomplete results; ensure sufficient data to support conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose target journal early and follow its instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you start writing, preferably choose the journal to which you will submit and plan the article to fit the journal’s preferred format (length, number of figures, style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain the journal’s instructions to authors and tailor abstract length, reference style, structure, and other format-specific requirements accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts should be COMPLETE, i.e. no necessary information should be missing; information is interpreted more easily if it is placed where readers expect to find it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure all standard sections and key details are present; follow conventional placement of information (title, abstract, methods, results, discussion, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Title
rubrics_metrics.description: Title should be unambiguous, understandable to specialists in other fields, and must reflect the content of the article; be specific, not general or vague.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If relevant, include study period/location, international scientific name, or experimental design (e.g. randomized controlled trial). Information in the title need not be repeated in the abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship criteria and listing
rubrics_metrics.description: List all people who contributed substantially to study planning, data collection or interpretation and wrote or critically revised the manuscript and approved its final version; authors listed first should have contributed most.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplement names with affiliations (during the study), present address for correspondence, and provide e-mail addresses for all authors so they can be contacted easily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract content and type
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract should explain BACKGROUND, OBJECTIVES, METHODS, RESULTS (major data, relationships), and CONCLUSIONS; it must reflect the content of the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research reports: informative abstracts including actual results. Reviews/meta-analyses: indicative abstracts listing topics without outcomes. Do not refer to tables/figures or include references unless absolutely necessary. Use all keywords within the abstract for indexing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keywords
rubrics_metrics.description: Include all relevant scientific terms absent from the title; keep keywords specific; add general terms if interdisciplinary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In medical texts, use vocabulary found in the MeSH Browser.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Define all abbreviations used in the article, except those obvious to non-specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a list if required by editors. Define abbreviations at first use in the text and avoid excessive abbreviation use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why the study was needed and specify your research objectives or questions; start general and focus on the research questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set context and lead the reader to the specific aims of the study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods: completeness and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe in detail how the study was carried out (study area, data collection, criteria, origin of material, sample size, measurements, age/sex, equipment, data analysis, statistical tests, software).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider all factors that could have affected results. If citing a method described in a non-English or inaccessible source, explain it in detail. Ensure compliance with ethical standards (patient rights, animal testing, environmental protection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Results: present new results and avoid reuse of published data
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the new results of your study; published data should not be included in this section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention all tables/figures in text and number them in order. Ensure statistical analysis is appropriate. Do not fabricate, distort, exclude important data, or manipulate images (such actions may constitute scientific fraud).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion: answer questions, compare objectively, and discuss limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Answer the research questions and compare new results with published data objectively; discuss limitations and highlight main findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider findings contrary to your view and support positions only with methodologically sound evidence; end with major conclusions and practical significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgements and disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Mention people who contributed substantially but are not co-authors and acknowledge funding sources; disclose conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recommended funding statement wording; disclose financial or personal links with manufacturers or interested organizations; obtain consent from people named; acknowledge language professionals/statisticians but clarify they are not responsible for the final version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissions for reproduced materials
rubrics_metrics.description: If you reproduce previously published materials (e.g. figures), ask copyright owners for permission and mention them in captions or acknowledgements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain and document permission; cite appropriately in captions/acknowledgements.

rubrics_metrics.name: References: accuracy and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide sources for all information extracted from other publications and include data necessary to find them; for non-English publications give original title (transliterated) and, if possible, translation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid citing inaccessible data; do not include unpublished data in the references (describe in main body and obtain permission if necessary). Follow the journal's reference style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article structure flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A different article structure may be more suitable for theoretical publications, review articles, case studies, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt structure to the genre (e.g., reviews, theory papers, case reports) while retaining clarity and completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide non-English abstracts/summaries when useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Some publications include an abstract or longer summary in another language; this is useful in many fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider including translations to increase accessibility across audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow journal-specific instructions (abstract length, references, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember to comply with the journal’s instructions to authors in respect of abstract length, style of references, and other format requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check and apply journal-specific formatting and submission rules early in writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness: relevance and redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include information that is not relevant to your research questions; the number of cited works should not be excessive; do not copy substantial parts of previous publications or submit the same manuscript to more than one journal at a time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid redundant publication; secondary publications may be acceptable for different audiences with editors’ approval; delete obvious statements and redundant fragments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repetition across sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Information given in one section preferably should not be repeated in other sections, except obvious exceptions (abstract, figure legends, concluding paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid repeating long lists or data in text if presented in tables/figures; do not duplicate table data in figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tables and figures: necessity and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether all tables and figures are necessary; make them understandable without reference to the main body; omit uninformative data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not repeat data between tables and figures; define abbreviations and symbols in captions/footnotes; provide axis labels and units; use decimal points; consider text-tables for small data sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captions: informative but concise
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions to tables and figures must be informative but not very long; ensure similar data have similarly formatted captions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If similar data appear in multiple figures/tables, use similar caption formats for consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delete obvious/tautological statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferably delete obvious statements (e.g. “Forests are very important ecosystems.”) and other redundant fragments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove filler and self-evident claims that add no value to the reader’s understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations: definition and restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: If a long scientific term is frequently repeated, define its abbreviation at first use and then apply it consistently; do not use too many different abbreviations; do not abbreviate rarely used terms; avoid abbreviations in the abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an abbreviation list if required and define all non-obvious abbreviations in captions or footnotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerals and numeric style
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless required otherwise by the editors, use numerals for all numbers, i.e. also for one-digit whole numbers, except for zero, one (if without units), and other cases where misunderstanding is possible (e.g. at the beginning of a sentence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow journal-specific numeric conventions when in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text structure and sentence construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences generally should not be very long; structure should be relatively simple, with the subject close to its verb. Avoid abstract nouns; prefer direct constructions (e.g. “X was measured…”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overuse of passive voice, modify sentence structure in translations if needed, and ensure paragraphs are cohesive and logically organized with topic sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohesion and paragraphing
rubrics_metrics.description: The text should be cohesive, logically organized, and easy to follow; each paragraph preferably should start with a topic sentence, and following sentences should develop the topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear transitions and structure to guide the reader; see appendices on cohesion and simplicity for more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of parallel constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: English allows parallel constructions which facilitate understanding when comparing similar data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write parallel lists (e.g. “high in A, medium in B, low in C”) rather than inconsistent forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make figures/tables self-contained (labels, units, decimal point)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make figures and tables understandable without reference to the main body; use decimal points (not commas) and provide axis labels and units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In long numbers, use thin spaces between groups of three digits; abbreviate litre as L to avoid confusion with number 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text-tables for small data
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider using text-tables when presenting a small set of data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text-tables can be clearer and more space-efficient than graphical tables for small datasets.

rubrics_metrics.name: List punctuation in long lists
rubrics_metrics.description: In long lists (of abbreviations, etc.) preferably separate individual items by semicolons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Semicolons are intermediate between commas and full stops and help readability in long lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language choice and register
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever scientific terms are not necessary, preferably use commonly known words; avoid colloquial and idiomatic expressions and phrasal verbs which are difficult for non-native speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer straightforward vocabulary; avoid expressions that may not translate well for an international readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tense usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the past tense when describing how you performed your study and what you found; preferably use the present tense in general statements and interpretations or when writing about content of your article (especially tables and figures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply tense consistently according to function: methods/results = past; general statements/conclusions = present.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person vs impersonal phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write about yourself as “the author(s)”; use “we” or “I” if necessary, or expressions like “in this study”, “our results”, or “in our opinion”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use “this study” only for new results; refer to publications as “that study” or authors as “those authors” to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Which vs that and equivocal words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use “which” in non-defining clauses and “that” in defining clauses; when using equivocal words, ensure their meaning is obvious from context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise with clause-defining words and avoid ambiguous vocabulary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar: agreement and pronoun clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Check that verbs agree in number with their subjects and that references for all pronouns are clear, crucial in translations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review for irregular plurals and ambiguous pronoun antecedents; reading aloud helps check clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define uncommon/ambiguous scientific terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Define every uncommon or ambiguous scientific term at first use; list synonyms if helpful but use one term consistently thereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer formal nomenclature established by scientific organizations; if a term has no English synonym define it precisely and suggest an English translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proper English scientific terms and check false friends
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure you are using proper English scientific terms, preferably based on texts by native speakers; literal translations often produce false friends or non-existent words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If in doubt, check an English dictionary or compare multilingual results (e.g. via Wikipedia) to verify meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report percentages and comparisons clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting percentages, make clear what you regard as 100%; when writing about correlations/relationships, make clear which values are being compared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify denominators and comparative bases to avoid misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Units, dates, and numeric notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Système International (SI) units and Celsius are generally preferred; use decimal point (not comma); denote months as words or first three letters to avoid British/American date confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviate litre as L; avoid capital Roman numerals for centuries; check journal and regional conventions for spelling and date notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number grouping in long numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: In numbers exceeding 4 digits to the right or left of the decimal point, use thin spaces (not commas) between groups of three digits in either direction from the decimal point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids confusion between thousands separators and decimal commas in international readerships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic names and contextual detail
rubrics_metrics.description: If lesser-known geographic names are translated, mention the original name if possible (e.g. local name in parentheses); additional location/climate information may be useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide context so international readers unfamiliar with local classifications can understand the study setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for international readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember the text will be read mainly by foreigners who may be unaware of specific local conditions/classifications; add explanations as necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify local terms, systems, or common names; provide internationally approved names (e.g. species names) and synonyms for searchability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation and intonation
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the text aloud to check punctuation; intonation breaks necessary for proper understanding should be denoted with commas or other punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: punctuation can change meaning (e.g. “no more data are needed” vs “no, more data are needed”).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency in spelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Be consistent in spelling; follow either British or American rules for spelling and date notation and use that setting in word/grammar checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the target journal uses American or British spelling and conform to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer reading and revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask a thoughtful colleague to read the whole text to detect ambiguous fragments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use colleague feedback to identify unclear passages and potential translation issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure compliance with ethical standards (e.g. Declaration of Helsinki) regarding patient rights, animal testing, and environmental protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose conflicts of interest and follow COPE/ORI guidance on plagiarism and scientific misconduct; follow appropriate ethical approval and consent procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid plagiarism and self-plagiarism; attribute sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly distinguish original data and ideas from others' and from your earlier publications; provide citations and paraphrase when possible; put literal copies in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to attribute may be plagiarism or self-plagiarism; follow ORI and COPE flowcharts and cite permissions when using unpublished or externally produced data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure statistical analysis is appropriate and reported clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to statistical guidance (e.g. Lang 2004) and ensure tests and software used are documented in Methods.
